title: Section check: Civics, Media & Everyday Economics
intro: 10 questions about Lessons 20–24. Take your time. You can look back at the lessons and try again as often as you like.

questions.question: Which of these is a need, not a want?

options.text: Music videos on a phone
options.feedback: Not quite. Music videos are nice, but you can live without them. That makes them a want. Look back at Lesson 20.

options.text: A new football
options.feedback: Not quite. A new football is fun, but you can live without it. That makes it a want. Look back at Lesson 20.

options.text: Clean water to drink
options.feedback: Yes. You must have clean water to live and stay healthy. That makes it a need.

stimulus.title: A made-up choice
stimulus.body: Amani and two friends share one tablet at a made-up learning centre. They have 30 minutes left on it today. They can play a word game or watch a short science video. There is not enough time for both. They choose the science video.

questions.question: What is the opportunity cost of their choice?

options.text: The word game they do not play
options.feedback: Yes. The word game is the next-best thing they give up. That is their opportunity cost.

options.text: The science video they watch
options.feedback: Not quite. The video is what they choose. The opportunity cost is what they give up. Look back at Lesson 20.

options.text: The tablet that they all share
options.feedback: Not quite. The tablet is a resource they use. The opportunity cost is the thing they give up. Look back at Lesson 20.

questions.question: Here is a made-up example. Jun fixes a broken chair for Lucia. In return, Lucia teaches Jun a card game. No money is used. What is this kind of exchange called?

options.text: Scarcity
options.feedback: Not quite. Scarcity means there is not enough for every use. Here, two people swap skills with no money. Look back at Lesson 21.

options.text: Barter
options.feedback: Yes. Barter means swapping a thing or a skill without using money. Jun and Lucia swap skills.

options.text: A budget
options.feedback: Not quite. A budget is a plan for money or time. Here, two people swap skills with no money. Look back at Lesson 21.

questions.question: Lesson 21 says every exchange depends on trust. What happens when a seller cheats?

options.text: More people want to buy from them.
options.feedback: Not quite. People do not want to buy from someone who cheats. Look back at Lesson 21.

options.text: People stop trusting the seller.
options.feedback: Yes. If someone cheats, people stop trusting them. Then trade gets harder for everyone.

options.text: Nothing changes at the market at all.
options.feedback: Not quite. Cheating breaks trust, and then trade gets harder for everyone. Look back at Lesson 21.

questions.question: Mei's time budget has 15 minutes for reading English and 15 minutes for games on the shared phone. What does this show?

options.text: A budget can plan time, not only money.
options.feedback: Yes. Budgets are not only for money. Mei uses a budget to plan her time in the evening.

options.text: A budget means Mei can never play games.
options.feedback: Not quite. Mei still has 15 minutes for games. She just has less time for them. Look back at Lesson 22.

options.text: A budget is only ever a plan for money.
options.feedback: Not quite. Mei's budget is a plan for her time. Budgets are not only for money. Look back at Lesson 22.

questions.question: Lesson 22 says that small, short goals are useful. Why?

options.text: They do not need any steps or plan.
options.feedback: Not quite. You still work towards a goal step by step. Look back at Lesson 22.

options.text: They make sure nothing will ever change.
options.feedback: Not quite. Plans can still change. That is why a small goal you can work on now helps. Look back at Lesson 22.

options.text: You can start to work on them now.
options.feedback: Yes. Plans can change, but you can work on a small goal now. One example is learning 10 new words a week.

stimulus.title: Message F, a made-up message from Lesson 23
items: A photo of a fish as long as a bus.
The words say: “Caught at Lakeside yesterday.”
The edges of the fish look strange.
Nobody else has a photo of this fish.

questions.question: Which detail is a clue that the photo may not be real?

options.text: It is a photo, not a written message.
options.feedback: Not quite. A photo can be real or changed. Being a photo does not show it is fake. Look back at Lesson 23.

options.text: The edges of the fish look strange.
options.feedback: Yes. Strange edges can show that a photo was changed with an app. Also, nobody else has a photo of this fish.

options.text: It says where the fish was caught.
options.feedback: Not quite. Naming a place does not show a photo is fake. Think about how the fish itself looks. Look back at Lesson 23.

stimulus.title: A made-up message
stimulus.body: Pia plays in a football team. She sees a message in a group chat. It says: “Our match at City Park is now on Sunday. Tell the whole team.” The message has no name and no date. Pia does not know who wrote it.

questions.question: What is the best thing for Pia to do first?

options.text: Send it to the whole team right now
options.feedback: Not quite. The message has no name or date, so Pia cannot trust it yet. It is safer to check first. Look back at Lesson 23.

options.text: Believe it, because it sounds very sure
options.feedback: Not quite. A message can sound sure and still be wrong. Pia needs to check it first. Look back at Lesson 23.

options.text: Ask her coach if the message is true
options.feedback: Yes. Her coach is a trusted source. Pia can verify the message before she shares it.

questions.question: Lesson 24 says the bus users are stakeholders. What does that word mean?

options.text: A person or group that a problem affects
options.feedback: Yes. The litter at the bus stop affects the bus users and the centre manager. So they are stakeholders.

options.text: A person who sells goods at a market stall
options.feedback: Not quite. The bus users are not selling anything. A stakeholder is someone a problem or plan affects. Look back at Lesson 24.

options.text: A person who checks if a message is true
options.feedback: Not quite. Checking messages is part of Lesson 23. A stakeholder is someone a problem or plan affects. Look back at Lesson 24.

questions.question: What does Lesson 24 say about ways to help a community?

options.text: Small, everyday actions can make a difference.
options.feedback: Yes. Reading with a younger child or keeping a shared room clean can help a community.

options.text: Only big campaigns can make a real difference.
options.feedback: Not quite. Helping does not have to mean a big campaign. Everyday actions matter too. Look back at Lesson 24.

options.text: You must speak in public to help at all.
options.feedback: Not quite. You never need to speak in public, post online or take risks to help. Look back at Lesson 24.

results.high: Well done. You know a lot about making choices, checking messages and helping a community.
results.middle: Good work. You got many questions right. Look back at the lessons for the ones you missed, and try again if you like.
results.low: Thank you for trying. Look back at Lessons 20–24, then try again. You can take as long as you need.
